message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. While this overview isn’t exhaustive, it covers many key points you should know: | Area | What It Means for You | |------|-----------------------| | **Security Deposits** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent (or two if the lease is longer than 12 months).
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | | **Habitability & Repairs** | • Landlords must keep the property safe, sanitary, and in good repair.
• If repairs are needed, you can request them in writing; landlords usually have 30 days to respond. | | **Rent Increases** | • For most residential leases, landlords can raise rent at the end of each lease term.
• For month‑to‑month agreements, they need 30 days’ notice before raising rent. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow a formal eviction process (notice, court filing, judgment).
• Common reasons include non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or landlord’s own use of the unit. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Tenants have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other occupants. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Under federal Fair Housing law and Texas statutes, discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc., is prohibited. | | **Lease Terms** | • Written leases are required for rentals over 90 days.
• Lease terms must be clear and cannot violate public policy. | | **Notice Requirements** | • Notice periods vary: 30 days for non‑renewal, 60 days for termination of a lease, 30 days for rent increase notices, etc. | | **Utilities & Maintenance** | • Clarify who pays utilities in your lease.
• Landlords must maintain essential services (heat, hot water, plumbing). | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting only with landlord approval.
• Subletting can affect liability for damages. | | **Move‑Out Inspection** | • Landlords often conduct a walk‑through inspection.
• Document the condition of the unit when you leave to avoid disputes. | ### Practical Steps 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all obligations, including payment schedules, pet policies, and maintenance responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of receipts, emails, text messages, and photos of the unit’s condition. 3. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities in Texas have additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoriums). 4. **Use the Texas Attorney General’s “Tenant Rights” Guide** – A free resource that explains rights and responsibilities in plain language. ### When Things Go Wrong - **Unlawful Eviction**: If you believe an eviction is unlawful, you can file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek legal counsel. - **Landlord Violations**: Report serious habitability issues to local health or building inspectors. If the landlord fails to act, you might be able to withhold rent or pursue a claim in small claims court. --- #### Quick Reference: Key Statutes | Statute | Relevance | |---------|-----------| | Texas Property Code §§ 92.001–92.021 | Security deposits | | Texas Property Code § 92.052 | Habitability requirements | | Texas Property Code § 92.051 | Landlord’s duty to maintain premises | | Texas Property Code § 92.053 | Right to quiet enjoyment | | Texas Property Code § 92.054 | Discrimination protections | | Texas Property Code § 92.055 | Notice requirements for lease termination | If you’re facing a specific issue—like a dispute over a security deposit, a potential eviction notice, or a maintenance problem—feel free to ask more detailed questions. I’m here to help clarify the relevant laws and suggest next steps!
